item.title: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection: implications for women's health, clinical care, and future research
item.description:
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an increasingly recognised cause of acute coronary syndromes, characterised by spontaneous separation of the layers of the coronary arterial wall. It predominantly affects younger women, and recent registry and imaging studies indicate that SCAD is more common than previously appreciated, challenging its historical classification as a rare condition. Clinically, SCAD is associated with a substantial early risk of adverse events, particularly in the first weeks after the index dissection. Given the high frequency of spontaneous healing, conservative management is preferred for most patients, whereas revascularisation is generally reserved for ongoing ischaemia or haemodynamic compromise. However, evidence to guide both pharmacological and interventional management remains scarce. This Review summarises current evidence on SCAD epidemiology, underlying mechanisms including genetic susceptibility, diagnostic approaches, management principles, implications for reproductive and women's health, and research priorities to improve outcomes for affected patients.

item.title: Seasonal mass vaccination for malaria control in west Africa
Seasonal mass vaccination with R21/Matrix-M against malaria in The Gambia and Burkina Faso: an open-label, cluster-randomised, controlled trial
item.description:
Background: The R21/Matrix-M (R21) malaria vaccine candidate, recommended by WHO for use in young children, could be extended to the whole population. Seasonal mass vaccination (SMV) before peak malaria transmission could be a promising tool to accelerate progress towards malaria elimination. We aimed to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of SMV with R21 in two malaria-endemic settings in west Africa.

Methods: This open-label, cluster-randomised, controlled trial was conducted in The Gambia, a setting with low-to-moderate seasonal transmission, and Burkina Faso, a setting with intense seasonal transmission. 54 medium-sized villages (30 in The Gambia and 24 in Burkina Faso) were randomly assigned (1:1) by use of computer-restricted randomisation to receive either SMV with R21 (intervention group) or no SMV (control group). All study villages received national standard malaria control interventions. In the intervention group, residents who were aged 5 months and older, willing to comply with trial procedures, and could provide written informed consent (from parents or guardians for children aged <18 years plus assent for children aged 12-17 years) were eligible for vaccination. The intervention was delivered as three monthly doses of 5 μg (participants aged <15 years) or 10 μg (participants aged ≥15 years) R21 plus 50 μg of Matrix-M. The primary outcome was malaria prevalence at peak transmission, defined as the proportion of participants with Plasmodium falciparum infection assessed by quantitative PCR. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06578572) and the Pan-African Clinical Trials Registry (PACTR202404544467702), and is ongoing.

Findings: The intervention was delivered between May 30, and Aug 21, 2024. A cross-sectional survey to estimate the primary endpoint was conducted between Nov 18 and Dec 6, 2024. The population available for vaccination varied across the three rounds. In The Gambia, among 4311 total residents in intervention villages, 2565 (59·5%) received three vaccine doses; in Burkina Faso, among 6235 total residents in intervention villages, 4072 (65·3%) received three vaccine doses. SMV with R21 reduced the odds of malaria infection by 70% (adjusted odds ratio 0·30 [95% CI 0·20-0·44]; p<0·0001) in The Gambia and by 25% (0·75 [95% CI 0·58-0·98]; p=0·036) in Burkina Faso. In The Gambia, prevalence decreased across all age groups, whereas in Burkina Faso the largest effect was observed in children younger than 5 years. The vaccine was safe and well tolerated. 651 adverse events were reported in 581 (13·5%) vaccine recipients in The Gambia, and 795 adverse events were reported in 705 (11·3%) vaccine recipients in Burkina Faso. Among 69 serious adverse events reported overall, only one was considered related to vaccination (febrile convulsions in a female participant aged 8 years after the second dose in The Gambia).

Interpretation: SMV with R21 reduced malaria prevalence in both settings. It could become an additional strategy for malaria control in endemic areas of seasonal transmission. In low-to-moderate transmission settings, the vaccine could accelerate progress towards elimination; in high-transmission areas it could further reduce the malaria burden.

Funding: UK Medical Research Council and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.

Dabira ED, Natama HM, Erhart A, Bihoun B, Keita ML, Derra K

Natural ligand-based CAR T-cell therapy targeting BCMA and TACI for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma (TriPRIL): a non-randomised, phase 1, first-in-human trial
item.description:
Background: Functional loss of B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) is a recognised mechanism of relapse after BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma. Targeting multiple tumour antigens simultaneously with a single CAR has the potential to mitigate antigen escape and prolong disease responses. Transmembrane activator and CAML interactor (TACI) and BCMA are both highly expressed on most myeloma cells and bind to the same natural ligand-a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL). We designed TriPRIL, a CAR that uses an engineered trimeric form of APRIL, to target both BCMA and TACI. We aimed to establish the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, and recommended phase 2 dose of autologous TriPRIL CAR T cells.

Methods: In this first-in-human, open-label, dose-escalation and dose-expansion, phase 1 study, we evaluated TriPRIL in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma at Massachusetts General Hospital (Boston, MA, USA). Eligible patients had received at least three previous lines of therapy or had triple-class refractory disease. Previous CAR T-cell therapy and bispecific antibody therapy exposure were permitted. Patients received 3 days of lymphodepletion with intravenous cyclophosphamide (300 mg/m2) and intravenous fludarabine (30 mg/m2) daily on days -5, -4, and -3 before intravenous TriPRIL infusion on day 0. In the dose escalation phase, patients received 1·0 × 108 or 3·0 × 108 TriPRIL CAR T cells to establish the recommended phase 2 dose, which was further evaluated in the dose expansion phase. The primary endpoint was the incidence of study-related adverse events (graded according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5) and dose-limiting toxicities in all patients who received an infusion of TriPRIL CAR T cells, until study completion at 24 months or progressive disease. The data cutoff date was March 24, 2026, when all infused patients had completed at least one assessment of disease response. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05020444), has fully accrued, and is ongoing.

Findings: Between Sept 17, 2021, and Jan 27, 2026, 16 patients were enrolled and underwent leukapheresis, with 15 patients subsequently receiving a TriPRIL cell infusion. Ten (67%) of 15 infused patients were female, five (33%)were male, and the median age was 69 years (IQR 65-75). Nine (60%) of 15 infused patients had previously received BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy, and four (27%) had previously received a BCMA-directed or GPRC5D-directed bispecific T-cell engager. Six patients were treated with 1·0 × 108 CAR T cells, and nine were treated with 3·0 × 108 CAR T cells; there were no dose-limiting toxicities at either dose. The most common adverse events were neutropenia (14 [93%] of 15 patients), nausea (12 [80%]), hypogammaglobulinaemia (eight [53%]), fatigue (seven [47%]), and fever (seven [47%]). Non-haematological adverse events grade 3 or worse occurred in five (33%) patients and all resolved. Cytokine release syndrome (grade 1 or 2 only) occurred in 13 (87%, 95% CI 60-98) infused patients. One (7%, 0-32) patient had grade 2 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and one (7%, 0-32) had grade 2 immune effector cell-associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome; both of these patients had received 3·0 × 108 CAR T cells, and both conditions resolved with corticosteroids. Infections occurred in six (40%, 16-68) infused patients, with a grade 3 infection in one patient (7%, 0-32). There were no treatment-related deaths. The recommended phase 2 dose of CAR T cells was set as 3·0 × 108 cells.

Interpretation: TriPRIL showed a favourable safety profile and warrants further investigation in patients with relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, including those previously treated with BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy. The study findings support further development of this dual-targeted, natural ligand-based CAR T-cell approach.
